passages.text:
**Abstract.** The Stieltjes measure of every integrable minimiser of the
zero-temperature Parisi functional for the pure, zero-field
Sherrington–Kirkpatrick model has full support on $[0,1)$ and a smooth
density that is strictly positive on $(0,1)$. We reconstruct OpenAI's quantitative
argument, organised around two uses of one spatial-moment inequality.
On a positive constant interval, it makes the derivative of the gradient
second moment strictly convex, contradicting the endpoint conditions
imposed by minimality. A separate boundary estimate excludes terminal
gaps. Full support then gives moment identities and smoothness; a local
constant replacement transfers the inequality to the minimiser and
forces its density to be positive. H.-B. Chen previously proved full support
and smooth nonnegative density. We explain the construction and uses of
the quantitative estimate while importing its shape comparisons and
full polynomial identity. We also derive the scalar value identity and
state the classical optimisation consequence and the additional steps
leading to asymptotically optimal quantum approximate optimization
algorithm (QAOA) circuits.
passages.rationale: The main result and the second use remain source arguments under the pure zero-field SK and integrable-minimiser hypotheses. The reconstruction genre and Chen attribution are preserved. The revised closing sentence selects algorithmic consequences as an outlook, without claiming a new theorem or a density premise for the algorithms.

passages.text: [Auffinger, Chen and Zeng (2020), Theorem 1][ACZ] proved infinite support. This need not be full support: the measure $\sum_{k\geq1}2^{-k}\delta_{1-2^{-k}}$ has infinitely many atoms and many gaps. [H.-B. Chen (2026), Theorem 1.3][Chen] subsequently proved full support and smooth nonnegative density. We follow OpenAI's quantitative proof of the support conclusion and its further strict-positivity result. The feature used twice is a lower bound valid throughout every positive constant interval of an admissible coefficient, without a minimising assumption. **Theorem 1 (full support; [OpenAI (2026a), Theorem 1.1][FS]).** If $\gamma\in\mathcal U$ minimises $\mathcal P$, then $$ \operatorname{supp}\mu_\gamma=[0,1),\qquad \gamma(t_2)>\gamma(t_1)\quad(0\leq t_10$. This second use needs the estimate for a local constant replacement that need not minimise, without requiring $q''=0$ at the comparison time. Its explicit positive margin must also survive the replacement's limit. Section 5 derives the scalar value formula and identifies the finite Gaussian observable used by the separate QAOA theorem. These optimisation consequences use full support; strict density positivity is a further analytic conclusion. We assume Itô calculus and martingale convergence. Omitted proofs are linked to *From Parisi full support to deterministic QAOA circuits: A long reasoning record*, the [companion edition of 26 October 2026](../long/reasoning-record.md); original-source citations remain beside the imported inputs.

passages.text: **Lemma 2 (constant-interval curvature; [OpenAI (2026a), Proposition 5.1][FS]).** Let $\gamma\in\mathcal U$, with its associated diffusion and moment $q$. If $\gamma=c$ on an open interval $I\subset(0,1)$, called a plateau, then for $t\in I$ $$ q'''(t)\geq\frac{c^2}{1000}\mathbb E[a(t,X_t)^4]>0 \quad\text{if }c>0. \tag{3} $$ If $c=0$, then $q''(t)=\mathbb E[\Phi_{xxx}(t,X_t)^2]>0$. Minimality is not a hypothesis of this lemma. Section 3 derives its moment polynomial and explains the integrated estimate imported from the source. **Proof of Theorem 1, assuming Lemma 2.** A complementary interval with two support endpoints admits two contact conditions; an initial interval without support at zero has coefficient zero; a terminal interval is handled here by a boundary estimate. Suppose $(\ell,r)$ is a support gap with endpoints in $S$ and $r<1$. The coefficient is a positive constant there: support at $\ell$ and absence of mass immediately to its right force $\mu_\gamma([0,\ell])>0$. Strict convexity of $q'$ and (2) give $$ q'(t)<\frac{r-t}{r-\ell}q'(\ell) +\frac{t-\ell}{r-\ell}q'(r)\leq1 \qquad(\ell0$, hence $q'(t)0$ and all $t$ sufficiently close to one. Two estimates produce this scale. The heat representation of the terminal value $|x|$ gives $1-u(t,x)^2\geq\kappa>0$ on $|x|\leq\sqrt{1-t}$. A transition-kernel comparison from a fixed earlier time gives a density $f_t(x)\geq m>0$ on the fixed window $|x|\leq1$, uniformly as $t\uparrow1$. Thus $$ 1-q(t)=\int_{\mathbb R}(1-u(t,x)^2)f_t(x)\,dx \geq2m\kappa\sqrt{1-t}. $$ The time-uniform density estimate, proved in Lemma 6.3, equations (6.6)–(6.7), is essential; pointwise positivity of each density would not suffice. For $h=1-t[long §5, “A shorter qualitative exclusion”](../long/reasoning-record.md#qualitative-terminal-gap). The boundary estimate retained here also describes the terminal behaviour of an arbitrary coefficient constant near one. The zero-coefficient heat argument and late-step variation have antecedents in [Chen, Handschy and Lerman (2018), Theorem 6 and its proof][CHL]. These cases exhaust the complement of the relatively closed set $S$. Consequently $S=[0,1)$, contact gives $q(t)=t$, and differentiation gives $\mathbb E a^2=1$, including the right-hand value at zero. Moreover, $\gamma(t_2)-\gamma(t_1)=\mu_\gamma((t_1,t_2])>0$. This proves Theorem 1 using the stated analytic inputs.

passages.text: The quantity used in both arguments is a spatial moment. Write $b=\Phi_{xxx}$ and $d=\Phi_{xxxx}$, and, for $00$. For its associated diffusion, $$ \mathcal C_\gamma(t)\geq\frac{c^2}{1000} \mathbb E[a(t,X_t)^4]. $$ Neither minimality nor a constant neighbourhood of $t$ is required. This is the consequence of [OpenAI (2026a), Proposition 5.1 and Lemmas 2.1–2.2][FS] stated in the companion's [Proposition 4.1, §4.5](../long/reasoning-record.md#fixed-time-coercivity). We first explain the positive-plateau estimate, then obtain this fixed-time form by inserting a short plateau. For a smooth coefficient the identity connecting the two applications is $$ q'''+2\gamma'\mathbb E a^3=\mathcal C_\gamma. $$ On a plateau, $\gamma'=0$; at a smooth minimiser, full support gives $q=t$ and hence $q'''=0$. Section 4 proves the required smoothness before using the second identity. On a plateau with $\gamma=c>0$, put $r=c\Phi_x=c u$, $v=r_x=c a$, $w=r_{xx}$ and $z=r_{xxx}$. This rescaling makes the derivative identities polynomial. The PDE becomes $r_t=-\tfrac12r_{xx}-rr_x$, and the diffusion has spatial generator $\tfrac12\partial_{xx}+r\partial_x$. Differentiating in space and applying Itô's formula gives the drift and diffusion pairs $(0,v)$, $(-v^2,w)$ and $(-3vw,z)$ for $r,v,w$, respectively. All expectations in this section evaluate spatial functions at $(t,X_t)$. Starting with $c^2q'=\mathbb E v^2$, Itô's formula gives $$ \begin{aligned} c^2q''&=\mathbb E[w^2-2v^3],\\ c^2q'''&=\mathbb E[z^2-12vw^2+6v^4] =c^2\mathcal C_\gamma(t). \end{aligned} \tag{4} $$ For example, the drifts of $w^2$ and $v^3$ are $z^2-6vw^2$ and $3vw^2-3v^4$, respectively. The negative mixed term is the obstacle. Convexity, which gives $v\geq0$, does not control it. Indeed, for the smooth auxiliary terminal value $\log(2\cosh x)$ and coefficient $\gamma\equiv1$, the solution is $\Phi(t,x)=\log(2\cosh x)+(1-t)/2$. Thus $r=\tanh x$; at $r^2=1/2$, the polynomial in (4) equals $-19/8$. This is a finite-step smoothing example, not a minimiser of the absolute-value-terminal problem; its calculation is given in [long §4.1](../long/reasoning-record.md#curvature-moments). The proof subtracts a spatial derivative whose expectation under the law of $X_t$ is zero. The resulting expression has a positive fourth-moment remainder. The backward value function and the forward density must satisfy joint shape restrictions for this decomposition to have the required signs. Those comparisons and the exact polynomial identity are the substantial inputs from [OpenAI (2026a), §§3–4][FS]. We explain their roles first for finite-step coefficients, then pass the integrated inequality to an integrable coefficient by approximation. Begin with a positive nondecreasing finite-step coefficient $\gamma_{\rm step}$: a function constant on each interval of a finite partition. Replace the terminal value $|x|$ by the smooth approximation $M^{-1}\log(2\cosh Mx)$, with $M\geq\|\gamma_{\rm step}\|_\infty$. On a step of height $c$, set $h=e^{c\Phi}$. Then $h_t=-h_{xx}/2$ and $r=h_x/h$. The same exponential removes the drift from the forward density equation. Indeed, writing $f=hg$ gives $$ \begin{aligned} f_t&=\tfrac12(hg)_{xx}-(h_xg)_x\\ &=-\tfrac12h_{xx}g+\tfrac12hg_{xx} =h_tg+\tfrac12hg_{xx}. \end{aligned} $$ Comparison with $f_t=h_tg+hg_t$ yields $g_t=g_{xx}/2$. Thus one backward heat factor and one forward heat factor determine the law against which the moment polynomial is integrated. For $s=-\partial_x\log g$, the source proves joint shape restrictions: on $x>0$, $r_x>0$ and $s_x\geq1/t$, both $r$ and $s$ are concave, and $H:=w/(2r)+v\leq0$ is nondecreasing. They also give $$ j:=s_x-(s/r)v=r\,\partial_x(s/r)\geq0. $$ The last inequality couples the backward gradient to the forward density; separate monotonicity and concavity do not supply it. On the first step, $s=x/t$, so concavity of $r$ gives $j\geq0$. A parabolic comparison propagates the sign within each step. At a forward jump with $k=c_+/c_-\geq1$, continuity of $\Phi$ and $f$ gives $$ r_+=kr_-,\qquad s_+=s_-+(k-1)r_-,\qquad j_+=(s_x)_+-\frac{s_+}{r_+}(r_x)_+=j_-. $$ The joint sign therefore survives coefficient jumps as well. The quotients $w/r$ and $s/r$ extend smoothly through zero because $r,s,w$ are odd and $r_x(0)>0$. The comparison's boundary controls and these extensions are analytic inputs from [OpenAI (2026a), Lemmas 3.2–3.4][FS], reconstructed in [long §4.3](../long/reasoning-record.md#shape-comparisons). The factorisation of the density gives $f_x/f=r-s$. For a suitable expression $F$ in the shape quantities, define $$ \mathcal W(F)=r\partial_xF+(v+r^2-rs)F. $$ Then $f\mathcal W(F)=\partial_x(rfF)$. The smooth extensions avoid an interior boundary term at zero, and the source's differentiated Gaussian tail estimates give $rfF\to0$ at both spatial infinities for the polynomial correction used below. Hence $\mathbb E_f\mathcal W(F)=0$, where $\mathbb E_f$ denotes integration against $f(x)\,dx$. The remaining step is algebra under these analytic restrictions. [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 4.1][FS] supplies an explicit polynomial $F_2$ and a decomposition $$ z^2-12vw^2+6v^4 =\mathcal W(F_2)+\kappa v^4+\mathcal R, \qquad \mathcal R\geq0,\qquad \kappa=\frac{1661507}{1521000000}>\frac1{1000}. $$ The coefficients of $F_2$ have both signs; no sign of $F_2$ or $\mathcal W(F_2)$ is needed, since the correction integrates to zero. In contrast, the shape inequalities make every term of $\mathcal R$ nonnegative. Two of its actual terms are $$ \frac{337}{10000}\,r^2j\,(-w/r-7v)^2, \qquad (2rH_x)v\left(\frac{2331}{10000}r^2+\frac{87}{2500}j\right). $$ The first needs the joint comparison $j\geq0$; the second also uses $H_x\geq0$ on the positive half-line. Reflection preserves these signs on the negative half-line. The remaining terms use $H\leq0$, forward concavity and the other shape bounds. Thus the decomposition is positive on the shapes supplied by the PDE, not on arbitrary spatial derivatives. Integration removes $\mathcal W(F_2)$ and keeps the fourth-moment margin, giving $$ \int_{\mathbb R}(z^2-12vw^2+6v^4)f\,dx \geq\frac1{1000}\int_{\mathbb R}v^4f\,dx. \tag{5} $$ We use (5) as an imported analytic estimate. The full polynomial and its decomposition are in [Lemma 4.1 and Table 1][certificate]; Proposition 4.2 integrates them using the signs and zero boundary flux supplied by Lemma 3.4. [Long §4.4, “How the signs make a correction with zero expectation useful”](../long/reasoning-record.md#curvature-algebra) reproduces the definitions and complete identity. To obtain Lemma 2 for an integrable coefficient, choose positive monotone step coefficients $\gamma_n$ retaining the plateau near a fixed interior time, with $\|\gamma_n-\gamma\|_1\to0$, and terminal parameters $M_n\geq\|\gamma_n\|_\infty$ with $M_n\to\infty$. Spatial derivatives through order four converge uniformly on a fixed strip below one, and the diffusions driven by the same Brownian motion converge (see [OpenAI (2026a), Lemmas 2.1–2.2 and Proposition 5.1][FS]). Only $v,w,z$ remain in (5), so no convergence theorem for the auxiliary logarithmic derivative $s$ is needed. Dividing by $c^2$ gives (3); strictness follows from $\Phi_{xx}>0$ on the plateau (see [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 2.3][FS]). The plateau-preserving approximants and their common strip bounds are specified in [long §4.5](../long/reasoning-record.md#plateau-limit). The zero plateau has the separate heat identity in Lemma 2. Its strictness uses a positive diffusion density and the fact that $\Phi_{xxx}$ cannot vanish identically: an even quadratic profile would contradict the one-Lipschitz bound and $|x|+O(1)$ growth. **Passage to a fixed time.** Now let $\gamma\in\mathcal U$ be continuous at $t\in(0,1)$, with $c=\gamma(t)>0$. For $0<\delta<\min(t,1-t)$ define $$ \gamma_\delta(s)= \begin{cases} c,&t-\delta\leq s0$, then $q'$ cannot attain an interior maximum. The endpoint slope bounds therefore give $q'<1$ inside the gap and the same strict area deficit. Proposition 3 supplies more for the next argument: it applies at the chosen comparison time without assuming $q''=0$, and its fourth-moment lower bound survives the local replacement. Bare strict positivity could be lost in that limit.

passages.text: Full support does not force pointwise positive density. For instance, $\gamma(t)=\int_0^t(s-\tfrac12)^2\,ds$ has full Stieltjes support but $\gamma'(\tfrac12)=0$: every interval of positive length has a positive integral, although the integrand vanishes at one point. The quantitative remainder in (5) rules this out for a minimiser. First, the identity $\mathbb E a^2=1$ expresses $\gamma$ as a quotient of continuous moments and then gives smoothness. Only afterwards do we apply the fixed-time spatial estimate to obtain $\gamma'>0$. **Corollary 4 (smooth positive density; [OpenAI (2026a), Corollary 6.4][FS]).** Under the hypotheses of Theorem 1, $\gamma(0)=0$ and $\gamma\in C^\infty([0,1))$, with derivatives at zero taken from the right. Its Stieltjes measure is $\mu_\gamma(dt)=\gamma'(t)\,dt$, and $$ 2\gamma'(t)\mathbb E[a(t,X_t)^3] \geq\frac{\gamma(t)^2}{1000}\mathbb E[a(t,X_t)^4]>0 \qquad(0[long §9.1](../long/reasoning-record.md#smooth-density-consequence). Now the two differentiated moments are $$ \frac{d}{dt}\mathbb E b^2=\mathbb E[d^2-6\gamma ab^2], \qquad \frac{d}{dt}\mathbb E a^3=\mathbb E[3ab^2-3\gamma a^4]. $$ For a smooth time coefficient, differentiating $q''=\mathbb E b^2-2\gamma\mathbb E a^3$ therefore gives $$ q^{(3)}+2\gamma'\mathbb E a^3 =\mathcal C_\gamma(t). \tag{9} $$ This identity displays the two uses of the same spatial moment. On a plateau, $\gamma'=0$ and $(v,w,z)=c(a,b,d)$ recover (4). For the now smooth minimiser, $q=t$, so $q^{(3)}=0$ and the left side is $2\gamma'\mathbb E a^3$. Proposition 3 supplies the lower bound for this spatial moment. Apply Proposition 3 to the now smooth minimiser. Strict increase and $\gamma(0)=0$ give $\gamma(t)>0$ for $t>0$; (9) therefore gives (7). Strictness follows from $\gamma(t)>0$ and $\mathbb E a^4\geq(\mathbb E a^2)^2=1$. In particular, Cauchy–Schwarz gives $$ \mathbb E a^3\leq\sqrt{\mathbb E a^2\,\mathbb E a^4} =\sqrt{\mathbb E a^4}\leq\mathbb E a^4, $$ so the same inequality implies $\gamma'(t)\geq\gamma(t)^2/2000$ for $0[Long §§9.1–9.2](../long/reasoning-record.md#smooth-density-consequence) retain the smoothness argument and fixed-time transfer, including the common approximation bounds. **Relation to earlier estimates.** The backward shape comparisons, transformed density and positive-temperature gap-crossing argument appear in [Lopatto (2026), v3, Propositions 3.6, 7.1 and 9.1][Lopatto]. [H.-B. Chen (2026), Proposition 4.2][Chen] proves the zero-temperature crossing implication $q''=0\Rightarrow q'''>0$ under the minimiser convention of §3.1. The quantitative bound (3) holds throughout a positive plateau of any admissible coefficient. Arbitrary-coefficient scope alone does not distinguish it from the later literature: [Lopatto's v4, Proposition 5.1 and Corollary 5.6][Lopatto-v4] give qualitative crossing for arbitrary positive-temperature probability measures. [Lopatto's external-field paper, Theorem 2.3, §8 and Appendix B][Lopatto-field] also uses a fixed-time spatial inequality for both support and density, with different terminal data, one-sided coefficient bounds and scalar hypotheses. The distinction relevant here is the fourth-moment margin available without a stationarity condition at the comparison time. The precise edition and hypothesis comparisons are in [long §2.3](../long/reasoning-record.md#prior-work-comparison).

passages.text: ### 5.1 The scalar value The support identities give a scalar representation of $P_*$. Set $M_t=u(t,X_t)$, the bounded gradient martingale satisfying $dM_t=a(t,X_t)\,dB_t$. The quadratic variations distinguish the two Hessian moments: $$ d\langle M\rangle_t=a(t,X_t)^2\,dt, \qquad d\langle M,B\rangle_t=a(t,X_t)\,dt. $$ Full support gives $\mathbb E a(t,X_t)^2=1$, hence each increment $M_t-M_s$ has unconditional variance $t-s$. This normalises the discrete increments below. The first moment of $a$ instead gives covariance with the driving noise. Let $U$ be the almost-sure and $L^2$ limit of $M_t$. The value identity is $$ P_*=\mathbb E[UB_1] =\int_0^1\mathbb E[a(t,X_t)]\,dt. \tag{10} $$ Boundedness gives $|U|\leq1$, while $\mathbb E M_t^2\to1$ gives $\mathbb E U^2=1$; therefore $U^2=1$ almost surely. To see the cancellation behind (10), the terminal convergence of the convex value functions gives $UX_1=|X_1|$, while Itô's formula gives $\mathcal P(\gamma)=\mathbb E|X_1|-\int_0^1t\gamma(t)\,dt$. Multiplying $X_1=B_1+\int_0^1\gamma(t)M_t\,dt$ by $U$ cancels that integral because $\mathbb E[UM_t]=t$. The Parisi formula then gives (10). The endpoint limits and stochastic-integral covariance are proved in [OpenAI (2026a), Corollary 7.1][FS] and the long record, [§6, “Recovering the value from a martingale”](../long/reasoning-record.md#scalar-value-identities). This argument uses full support, not the density corollary. In particular, convexity and Cauchy–Schwarz give $0\leq\mathbb E a\leq1$, so $$ 0\leq P_*-\int_0^T\mathbb E[a(t,X_t)]\,dt\leq1-T. $$ One can therefore fix the terminal cutoff before discretising the diffusion. The gradient-martingale and value methods have antecedents in [Montanari, preprint v2, Lemmas 3.2–3.4][Montanari], under its positive-temperature support assumption, and in the zero-temperature calculations of [El Alaoui, Montanari and Sellke, preprint v1, Lemmas 6.5 and 6.13][EAMS]. [Sellke, preprint v4, Proposition 3.10 and Lemma 3.11, p. 17][Sellke] gives the closely related finite-cutoff cancellation by applying Itô's formula to $\Phi$ and $x\Phi_x$. ### 5.2 The classical algorithm Full support and existence give an attained, strictly increasing minimiser in the monotone zero-temperature class. This is Assumption 2 of [El Alaoui, Montanari and Sellke, preprint v1][EAMS]. Their Corollary 2.2 then gives, for every fixed $\varepsilon>0$, a randomised algorithm returning a configuration within $\varepsilon n$ of the finite SK maximum with probability tending to one over couplings and algorithmic randomness. Its cost is $C(\varepsilon)n^2$ real-arithmetic operations with the prescribed scalar functions and normalisers available; this includes no separate numerical-preprocessing or finite-precision bound. [OpenAI (2026a), Corollary 7.3][FS] and [long §9.4](../long/reasoning-record.md#classical-algorithm-consequence) check the Gaussian convention and operation count. Chen already records the classical consequence in [§1, p. 4][Chen]. In their incremental approximate message-passing construction, the noise and drift coefficients are, in our notation, $$ u_{\rm EAMS}(t,x)=a(t,x),\qquad v_{\rm EAMS}(t,x)=\gamma(t)u(t,x). $$ Thus their noise multiplier is the Hessian, whereas our $u$ is the gradient. The bounded martingale $M_t$ and $\mathbb E a^2=1$ give the required variance normalisation. With the fixed-strip regularity and discretisation estimates, [their Theorem 2][EAMS] achieves energy arbitrarily close to the truncated first-moment integral in (10). Strict positivity of the density is unnecessary.

passages.text: ### 5.3 A fixed QAOA circuit before the thermodynamic limit Let $\widehat Z_i,\widehat X_i$ be Pauli operators, and define the cost and mixer by $$ C_{n,J}=\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i0$ there is one finite $W$ with $v(W)\geq P_*-\varepsilon$, whose depth and angles depend on $\varepsilon$ but not on $n$ or $J$. The instance still determines $C_{n,J}$. Here depth counts global cost–mixer layers; their elementary gate counts depend on the implementation. This order of limits differs from the fixed-instance depth limit in [Farhi, Goldstone and Gutmann, §VI][FGG], which permits instance-dependent choices. The common-circuit conclusion was conjectured by [Basso, Farhi, Marwaha, Villalonga and Zhou (2022), §7, equation (7.2)][BFMVZ]. **The finite Gaussian input.** Fix the minimiser and its diffusion, a cutoff $0[long §7, “A finite Gaussian spin and its adjacent correlations”](../long/reasoning-record.md#finite-gaussian-approximation). **The rooted energy and its circuit realisation.** The next identity comes from a separate construction in [OpenAI (2026b), §2 and Lemma 3.1][Q]. Its classical sector consists of square-integrable functions built recursively from a local Gaussian seed and Gaussian coordinates generated by child functions; the inner product is expectation. Centred real child directions have lifts $\mathsf G(f)$ at the receiving root that form a centred Gaussian family with $$ \mathbb E[\mathsf G(f)\mathsf G(g)]=\langle f,g\rangle. $$ The receiving root's seed is independent of these coordinates. Compatible embeddings compare functions of different finite depths without changing earlier variables. The root shift $\mathsf L$ inserts a child direction into the first Gaussian chaos (the linear Gaussian part), with constant receiving-root state; its adjoint projects onto that part and returns the child direction. This representation builds on the fixed-depth spin–boson description of [Boulebnane et al. (2026)][spin-boson]. Start with the root seed $g_0$ and recursively put $Z_{j+1}=\mathsf G(g_j)$. The orthonormal child directions give independent standard Gaussian lifts, reproducing the scalar law. The finite spin $F_N$ depends only on those lifts. Projection therefore gives the exact rooted-energy identity $$ \begin{aligned} \mathsf L^*F_N&=\sum_{j=0}^N\mathbb E[F_NZ_{j+1}]g_j,\\ \mathcal E(F_N):=\operatorname{Re}\langle F_N,\mathsf L F_N\rangle &=\sum_{j=0}^N\mathbb E[F_Ng_j]\,\mathbb E[F_NZ_{j+1}] =S_{T,N}. \end{aligned} \tag{12} $$ Independence of the receiving-root seed removes the $j=0$ term. This identity concerns the finite Gaussian formula in a limiting rooted space, not a finite-$n$ circuit. The unshifted pairing can have the same scalar limit without identifying this energy. The construction and projection are proved in [long §8.1](../long/reasoning-record.md#rooted-energy). **Proposition 5 (circuit approximation; a consequence of [OpenAI (2026b), §§2–5][Q]).** For each fixed $T,N$ in the preceding construction with finite positive normalisers, and every $\eta>0$, there is a finite ordinary QAOA word $W$, with deterministic angles independent of $n$ and $J$, such that $$ |v(W)-S_{T,N}|<\eta. $$ This imports the circuit construction for these particular Gaussian data. Bounded smooth odd approximations to the transmitted functions, together with exclusions on dependencies between seed classes, make the formula eligible for Theorem 4.1 while changing its rooted energy arbitrarily little. Smoothing the final sign alone is insufficient. That theorem synthesises the formula with temporary Gaussian seed controls, reusing the same sitewise seeds throughout the word. Theorem 5.1 removes their joint effect using cost and mixer gates. Proposition 2.1 identifies the resulting fixed word's tree energy with $v(W)$. The absolute approximation bounds give Proposition 5; [long §§8.1–8.6](../long/reasoning-record.md#qaoa-construction) retain the eligibility conditions and proofs. The deduction of near-optimality is now explicit: $$ P_*-v(W)\leq (P_*-I_T)+|I_T-S_{T,N}|+|S_{T,N}-v(W)|. \tag{13} $$ Choose $T$ so that $1-T<\varepsilon/3$, then $N$ so that the second term is below $\varepsilon/3$, and finally use Proposition 5 with $\eta<\varepsilon/3$. These finite choices give $v(W)>P_*-\varepsilon$ before $n$ tends to infinity. The source's Appendix A supplies an alternative positive-temperature input to the same synthesis. The selected construction supplies no quantitative depth bound, finite-size rate or efficient procedure for finding angles. **Corollary 6 (a measured configuration on the same instance).** For every $\varepsilon>0$ there is a finite ordinary QAOA word $W_\varepsilon$, chosen independently of $n$ and $J$, such that one computational-basis measurement $\Sigma$ satisfies $$ \Pr_{J,\Sigma}\!\left\{ \max_\sigma H_{n,J}(\sigma)-H_{n,J}(\Sigma)\leq\varepsilon n \right\}\longrightarrow1 \qquad(n\to\infty). \tag{14} $$ **Proof.** For a fixed word, put $Y_n=H_{n,J}(\Sigma)/n$ and $K_n=\max_\sigma H_{n,J}(\sigma)/n$. [Farhi, Goldstone, Gutmann and Zhou, §4, equations (13)–(22)][FGGZ] prove $$ \mathbb E_{J,\Sigma}Y_n\to v(W),\qquad \mathbb E_{J,\Sigma}Y_n^2\to v(W)^2. $$ The second moment is $\mathbb E_J\langle(C_{n,J}/n)^2\rangle$, so it includes measurement variance as well as disorder fluctuations. Thus $Y_n\to v(W)$ in joint $L^2$. Gaussian concentration of the maximum and its defining mean limit give $K_n\to P_*$ in probability. Choose $W$ with $P_*-v(W)<\varepsilon/3$. With probability tending to one, both $K_n-P_*<\varepsilon/3$ and $v(W)-Y_n<\varepsilon/3$, which proves (14). The two energies use the same $J$; no independence between them is needed. The companion's [§11.2, “What is averaged, and a fixed-word probability consequence”](../long/reasoning-record.md#fixed-word-probability) gives the concentration argument and its further probability consequences.

passages.text: This AI-assisted article reconstructs the cited analytic arguments. The integrated estimate (5), its shape hypotheses and compact-strip approximation are substantial imported inputs.
